title: Suicide Risk Assessment and Urgent Mental-Health Crisis Pathway

evidenceAudit.scope: People of any age attending the emergency department, primary care or a ward after self-harm or with suicidal thoughts: immediate physical and safety assessment, early psychosocial assessment by a mental health professional, why risk scores must not decide care, safety planning, means restriction, children and young people, people who leave before assessment, and aftercare within 48 hours.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-22.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Saudi Mental Health Care Law (2014) provisions on emergency assessment, involuntary admission and consent were not opened in this session; follow the hospital policy issued under that law.
No Saudi Ministry of Health self-harm or suicide prevention pathway was located; national crisis line numbers must be added locally.
NICE NG225 Table and recommendation text for 1.7.18 and the full bullet list of 1.13.1 were not visible in the text opened.
The American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) policy was read from a guideline summary page, not the full journal article.
Medicines for overdose (for example acetylcysteine) and rapid tranquillisation are outside this topic and follow their own topics or local protocol.

pathophysiology.summary: Self-harm is any act of self-poisoning or self-injury, whatever the motive; it is a strong marker of later suicide, so every attendance needs a mental health assessment rather than a judgement of seriousness from the method. Distress, hopelessness and a recent crisis (relationship loss, debt, bereavement, legal problems) interact with access to means; removing means at the time of crisis lowers the chance of a fatal act. Suicide prediction tools have low positive predictive value, which is why NICE NG225 says they must not be used to predict suicide or to decide who receives treatment. Intoxication and physical injury can mask or delay the mental health picture, but NICE says assessment should not wait for medical treatment to finish or for alcohol levels to fall.

symptoms: Suicidal thoughts, with or without a plan or intent.
Recent self-poisoning or self-injury, including repeated episodes.
Hopelessness, feeling a burden, wish to die.
Recent crisis: loss, conflict, abuse, financial or legal problems.
physicalSigns: Injuries: cuts, burns, ligature marks; assess severity and urgency of treatment.
Signs of poisoning: drowsiness, vomiting, tachycardia, abnormal vital signs.
Withdrawn, distressed or agitated mental state.
Evidence of planning: note, preparation, choice of a lethal method.
redFlags: Wish to leave before psychosocial assessment or treatment is complete.
Current intent with access to lethal means.
Serious physical injury or a high-toxicity overdose.
Child or young person under 18 who has self-harmed: needs an experienced child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) professional.
Safeguarding concern, including abuse or exploitation.
Psychosis, severe depression or inability to engage in assessment.
precipitants: Mental illness, including depression, psychosis, eating disorder and substance misuse.
Recent loss, bereavement, relationship breakdown or isolation.
Chronic pain or serious physical illness.
Access to medicines, firearms, ligature points or heights.
Abuse, bullying or exploitation, especially in young people.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fluctuating attention and awareness with a medical cause; treat the cause and reassess mental state when clear.
Mental state changes as levels fall; NICE still advises agreeing immediate support and not using alcohol levels to delay assessment.
Clear unintentional mechanism confirmed with the person; if any doubt, manage as self-harm.
Hallucinations or delusions drive the act; needs urgent psychiatric treatment and may need assessment under mental health law.

ruleIn.targetCondition: Needs, safety concerns, mental illness and protective factors
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Current intent, plan, access to means, hopelessness, safeguarding issues and unmet needs that shape the care plan.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Do at the earliest opportunity and at every attendance; do not delay until medical treatment is complete or alcohol levels fall.
ruleIn.normalValue: No current suicidal intent or plan; supports and coping identified

clinicalManagement.title: Triage and immediate safety
actions: Establish injury severity and urgency of physical treatment, emotional state and distress, immediate safety and safeguarding concerns.
Establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing it with the person.
Seat the person in a waiting area close to staff; use a private area for assessment.
Treat with the same respect and compassion as any other patient.

clinicalManagement.title: Physical treatment in parallel
actions: Treat injuries and poisoning; take paracetamol level and alanine aminotransferase at 4 hours in any intentional self-poisoning.
Order other tests according to history and examination, not as a routine screen.
Assess capacity for any treatment decision and record it.

clinicalManagement.title: Liaison psychiatry and psychosocial assessment
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as possible after arrival, at every attendance
actions: Offer referral to age-appropriate liaison psychiatry at arrival.
Mental health professional sees and speaks to the person at every attendance.
Do not delay assessment until medical treatment is complete or alcohol levels fall.
Do not use risk tools, scales or low, medium or high labels to decide treatment or discharge; base the plan on needs and safety concerns.

clinicalManagement.title: Person wishes to leave before assessment
actions: Follow the department policy for people who have self-harmed and wish to leave.
Senior clinician and mental health professional assess capacity and immediate safety.
Use mental health law under hospital policy if criteria are met; inform security only as the policy states.
If the person leaves, contact them and their general practitioner and, where appropriate, family or carers.

clinicalManagement.title: Children and young people
actions: Assessment by a mental health professional experienced with children and young people who self-harm.
Admitted children on a paediatric ward have specialist mental health access, daily joint reviews and daily family access.
Young people aged 16 and 17 are cared for on a ward suited to their age and needs.
Act on safeguarding concerns.

clinicalManagement.title: Safety plan and aftercare
actions: Develop a safety plan with the person: warning signs, coping strategies, means restriction and crisis contacts; the person holds a copy.
Agree the purpose, format and frequency of aftercare and record it in the care plan.
Provide initial aftercare within 48 hours of assessment when safety concerns remain.
Review medicines with the person: limit quantities and ask for unwanted medicines to be returned.

medicationPlan.note: NICE NG225 recommendation 1.11.10: do not offer drug treatment as a specific intervention to reduce self-harm. Treat any mental illness found on assessment under its own guideline. Antidotes for overdose (for example acetylcysteine for paracetamol) and rapid tranquillisation follow their own topics or local protocol. Review current prescriptions for toxicity in overdose and use shared decision making to limit quantities (recommendations 1.13.2–1.13.5).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Psychosocial assessment by a mental health professional at the earliest opportunity, at every attendance, without waiting for medical treatment to finish.
Do not label people as low, medium or high risk and do not use risk tools or scales to predict suicide or to decide treatment or discharge.
Within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment when safety concerns remain.
Assessment by a mental health professional experienced in assessing children and young people who self-harm.

guidelineComparison.title: Risk tools: NICE NG225 and ACEP compared

values: Do not use to predict suicide or repetition, or to decide who receives treatment or is discharged
Do not use currently available tools in isolation to identify low-risk patients safe for discharge

rows.parameter: Low, medium or high risk labels
values: Do not use global risk stratification to predict or to allocate treatment
Do not delay assessment for medical treatment or alcohol levels
Do not routinely order laboratory tests in alert patients with normal vital signs

guidelineComparison.note: Both sources reject risk scores as the basis for discharge; NICE goes further and removes them from treatment decisions altogether. This pathway follows NICE: the plan is built on the person's needs and safety concerns.

teaching.scope: People of any age attending the emergency department, primary care or a ward after self-harm or with suicidal thoughts: immediate physical and safety assessment, early psychosocial assessment by a mental health professional, why risk scores must not decide care, safety planning, means restriction, children and young people, people who leave before assessment, and aftercare within 48 hours.
learningObjectives: Carry out triage of physical and immediate safety needs after self-harm.
Arrange psychosocial assessment by a mental health professional without waiting for medical treatment to finish.
Explain why risk tools and low, medium or high labels must not decide care.
Build a safety plan with means restriction and crisis contacts.
Arrange aftercare within 48 hours when safety concerns remain.
pitfalls: Discharging on the basis of a low risk score.
Judging seriousness by the method or the medical severity of the act.
Letting a person leave without following the policy for those who wish to leave.
Prescribing large quantities of medicines toxic in overdose.
keyPoints: Every self-harm attendance gets a mental health assessment, whatever the method.
Risk scores do not predict suicide well enough to decide treatment or discharge.
Intoxication or ongoing medical treatment does not justify delaying assessment.
Take a paracetamol level in any intentional overdose.
Means restriction and a person-held safety plan are core interventions.

patientEducation: Explain what the assessment involves and that it is offered at every attendance.
Give the person a copy of their safety plan and crisis contact numbers, including the local emergency number.
With consent, involve family or carers in removing means and in knowing the warning signs.
lifestyleAndDiet: Reduce alcohol and drug use, which increase impulsive acts.
Keep regular sleep, contact with supportive people and daily structure.
Store medicines safely in limited quantities and return unwanted medicines to the pharmacy.
mdtReferrals: Child and adolescent mental health services for people under 18.
Community mental health or crisis team for aftercare.
General practitioner for follow-up and medicines review.
Social work and safeguarding team where needed.
Toxicology or poisons centre for overdose management.
dischargeCriteria: Psychosocial assessment completed by a mental health professional.
Physically fit for discharge with overdose treatment complete.
Safety plan agreed and held by the person.
Means restriction discussed and acted on.
Aftercare arranged, within 48 hours if safety concerns remain, and the general practitioner informed.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Initial aftercare within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment when safety concerns remain, then follow-up by the community mental health team or general practitioner as agreed in the care plan; review the safety plan and medicines at each contact.
